<!--- Provide a general summary of your changes in the Title above -->

#### Description
<!--- Describe your changes in detail -->
- Fix issue where resulting order quantity would place us higher than the target holding percentage
- Address order adjustment rounding problem

Note this is a "lighter" refactor version of the changes in #5702 that doesn't completely rewrite the function.  It aims to alleviate the issues in a similar way without a complete refactor. Those changes are still valid, and maybe in the future could be used as a refactor guideline as it is a bit more concise than this version.

#### Related Issue
<!--- This project only accepts pull requests related to open issues -->
<!--- If suggesting a new feature or change, please discuss it in an issue first -->
<!--- If fixing a bug, there should be an issue describing it with steps to reproduce -->
<!--- Please link to the issue here: -->
Closes #5687 

#### Motivation and Context
<!--- Why is this change required? What problem does it solve? -->

This bug was a interesting one, basically with the previous implementation it was possible to get values out of BuyingPowerModel.GetMaximumOrderQuantityForTargetBuyingPower() that would actually put us over our target holding percentage. This is because once we got our order margin and target margin set we would not consider the total holdings or whether the order was positive/negative for adjustments. 

For a specific definition of satisfying our portfolio target:

TargetHoldingsMargin => Amount in dollars the target holdings will cost -> TargetHoldings * UnitMargin
TargetMarginAllocated => Amount of portfolio dollars dedicated to this holding -> Target Percentage * (TotalPortfolioValue - RequiredFreeBuyingPower)

    ✅ TargetHoldingsMargin <= TargetMarginAllocated 
    
    Target holdings MUST be less than portfolio target, these values are absolutes so even if we have a short TargetMarginAllocated of -970, we require the TargetHoldingsMargin to be > -970.
